deep.reconstruction:
Setting (continuing the previous page): (α_n) is a decreasing sequence of positive numbers, and ρ is its 'order', i.e. its exponent of convergence. Equivalently ρ = inf{s : Σ α_n^s < ∞} = inf{s : α_n = O(n^{-1/s})}; the previous page proved these two characterisations agree. Assume now Σ α_n < ∞, so ρ ≤ 1, and put f(z) = ∏(1+α_n z). This is an entire function of genus 0, and since α_n > 0, M(r) = f(r). Claim: ρ equals the order of f, ord f = limsup_{r→∞} log log f(r) / log r.

(i) ρ ≤ ord f. This is the classical fact (Hadamard/Borel, via Jensen) that the convergence exponent of the zeros is at most the order. It is quoted as known for arbitrary α_n.

(ii) ord f ≤ ρ. First the model case α_n = n^{-β} with β > 1. Split f(r) = ∏_{n≤ν}(1 + r/n^β) · ∏_{n>ν}(1 + r/n^β).
- Tail: by 1+x ≤ e^x it is ≤ exp(R(ν) r), where R(ν) = Σ_{n>ν} n^{-β} ≤ ∫_ν^∞ x^{-β} dx = ν^{1-β}/(β-1).
- Choice of ν: take ν = [r^{1/β}] + 1. Then r ν^{1-β} ≤ r^{1/β}, so the tail is ≤ exp(C r^{1/β}).
- Head: it is ≤ (1+r)^ν = exp(ν log(1+r)), with ν ≈ r^{1/β}. Hence it also has order ≤ 1/β.
So ∏(1 + r n^{-β}) has order ≤ 1/β, and the margin notes it is in fact = 1/β.

General case (implicit, not written): if α_n ≤ C n^{-β}, then f(r) ≤ g(Cr), where g is the model product. Rescaling r does not change the order, so ord f ≤ 1/β for every 1/β > ρ, hence ord f ≤ ρ. The edge case ρ = 1 is trivial, since f(r) ≤ exp(r Σα_n).

The page ends by recalling that the order can also be computed from the maximal term B(r) = sup_n |a_n| r^n of the Taylor series.

Purpose: the next page extends this to complex α_i (using |α_i| and Hadamard's theorem). It then defines the 'order' of a sequence of complex numbers, and further of sequences in Banach/Fréchet spaces and of bounded sets and operators. This is the groundwork for the 1953–56 theory of s-nuclear operators ('opérateurs d'ordre s') and of the order of Fredholm determinants det(1+zu).
errors: The reduction from general decreasing α_n = O(n^{-β}) to the model case α_n = n^{-β} (by comparison and rescaling r) is not written out.
β > 1 is tacitly needed for R(ν) to be finite; this is consistent with the hypothesis Σα_n < ∞, i.e. ρ ≤ 1. The borderline case ρ = 1 is not mentioned but is trivial.
In the maximal-term formula, B(r) should be sup_n |a_n| r^n; the absolute value is missing. Here a_n ≥ 0, so it is harmless.
Otherwise the estimates (integral bound, choice ν = [r^{1/β}]+1, the inequality r ν^{1-β} ≤ r^{1/β}) are correct.

ideas.what: Order of a canonical product of genus 0 equals the exponent of convergence of its zeros
ideas.modern_name: Borel's theorem on canonical products / exponent of convergence = order (Hadamard–Borel)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Hadamard (1893), Borel (1897); standard in Titchmarsh, Levin, Boas
ideas.where_published: Classical; used implicitly in Grothendieck, 'La théorie de Fredholm', Bull. SMF 84 (1956)

ideas.what: Splitting the product at ν ≈ r^{1/β} and bounding the tail by exp(R(ν)r) and the head by (1+r)^ν
ideas.modern_name: Standard estimate of the maximum modulus of a canonical product

ideas.what: Order computed from the maximal term B(r) = sup |a_n| r^n
ideas.modern_name: Maximal term / Wiman–Valiron theory; order formula via the Taylor coefficients

ideas.what: Using the order of an entire function to motivate an 'order' of a sequence, later of sequences in Banach/Fréchet spaces and of operators
ideas.where_published: Produits tensoriels topologiques et espaces nucléaires (Memoirs AMS 16, 1955), ch. II; 'La théorie de Fredholm', Bull. SMF 84 (1956)

deep.surprise_reason: The page proves a classical textbook fact (order of a genus-0 canonical product = convergence exponent) by a standard splitting argument. Its only interest is as preparatory scaffolding for Grothendieck's published theory of operators of order s and Fredholm determinants.
transcription_corrections: Line 1: the crossed-out opening is probably 'Supposons maintenant'; the inserted text seems to read 'Alors ρ est aussi l'ordre de la fonction entière', with '0 < ρ' a marginal insertion.
'on sait que ρ est ≤ ordre de la fonction f(z), [pour (α_n)] arbitraire' — the gap likely refers to α_n being arbitrary.
The parenthetical after ≤ 1/β likely reads '(on sait d'ailleurs qu'on a = 1/β)'.
The upper limit of the first product is ν (nu), not v; the second product runs from ν+1 to ∞.
There is a left-margin note 'ν ≥ q' (or similar) near the 'En effet' line that the transcription omits.
B(r) = sup_n (a_n r^n): the subscript under sup is n.
